e.t: Abel is a proper name—the personal name of Adam and Eve’s son in Genesis. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears 13 times, chiefly in Genesis and 2 Samuel, and once in 4 Maccabees. Its first appearance is in Genesis 4:2, and the same name continues to identify him in later references. Because Abel is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader which person is being mentioned, while the surrounding passage supplies the details about him.

This noun means “purification”: the act or process of being made clean. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, chiefly in Numbers and once in Jeremiah. It names purification itself rather than describing a person, place, or object. As with any noun, its exact force in a particular passage is determined by the surrounding wording.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Anchous” or “Angghus.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel and a few in 1 Kings. The name itself does not provide a general concept or moral quality; its role is to identify the individual named in each passage. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which person is being discussed in a particular occurrence.

Aithi, also called Ethi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 11:31. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or description. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, not from an expanded definition of the name.

This Greek LXX noun means “story.” It names a story within a sentence, functioning as a thing or subject being mentioned rather than an action, quality, or description. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject.

Aitan, also rendered Etan, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person or place by name. It occurs once, in Joshua 15:59, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying use rather than a broader descriptive sense. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely whom or what the name identifies there.

“Ala” is a proper name used as a personal or place designation in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader abstract meaning. This name occurs 10 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across nine verses, including passages in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and Sirach. The surrounding verse is needed to identify exactly whom or what Ala designates in each occurrence.

This adjective describes someone or something belonging to another person, or someone regarded as a stranger or outsider. It can mark a distinction between what is one’s own and what belongs to someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 154 times, showing regular use for people, possessions, or things viewed as outside the immediate group or relationship. Its exact force in a verse depends on the noun and surrounding sentence, but its central idea is otherness, foreign belonging, or unfamiliar association.

Amasian is a proper name, used to identify a person rather than to express an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times: four times in 2 Chronicles and once in Amos. The name itself is rendered simply as “Amasian,” and the available information does not provide an additional definition or meaning beyond this personal designation. Its precise reference in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being discussed there.

This proper name refers to an Ammanite, a person associated with Ammanitis. In the Greek Old Testament, it functions as a people or national designation rather than a general description of character or action. It occurs seven times, all within Old Testament passages represented in the Greek LXX, including references in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Samuel, Chronicles, and Nehemiah. The precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means a “net,” referring to a physical net as an ordinary object. It is a noun, and its meaning remains concrete rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Psalms, Ecclesiastes, and Habakkuk. The same word appears repeatedly in Habakkuk, but its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as faultless—without blame or guilt. It identifies a person regarded as not responsible for wrongdoing, rather than naming an action or event. In the Greek Old Testament and Susanna, it occurs five times: four times in Deuteronomy and once in Susanna. Its basic sense remains concise and consistent, while the surrounding verse determines who is being described as faultless in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “stretch up” or “hold up.” It describes raising or extending something upward, whether by lifting it or keeping it raised. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what is being raised or supported in the surrounding text.

gl: take away from the opposite sides of an account; cancel
d: take away from the opposite sides of an account; cancel

e.t: This verb means to take away from the opposite sides of an account, thereby canceling it. It describes a balancing action in which corresponding amounts are removed so that an obligation or entry no longer stands. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, appearing eight times in Psalms and once in Esther. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is removal from both sides to cancel what is being counted.

This Greek LXX verb means to urge war against someone—to oppose them in an active, hostile way. It describes deliberate opposition rather than mere disagreement, and its verbal function points to an action directed against an opponent. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 41:12. The precise force in that verse belongs to its surrounding wording, but the word itself presents opposition as warfare or an appeal to wage war.

This Greek LXX noun describes someone who is foolish because he is unfamiliar with what is good or has no experience of goodness. The idea joins lack of understanding with lack of moral goodness, rather than merely describing someone who lacks information. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Esther 8:12. Since the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be read from the surrounding passage.

Asebia is a proper name, also given as “Asevia.” It identifies a specific named referent rather than expressing a general quality, action, or description. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise person or referent identified by the name cannot be described further. Its role is therefore best understood simply as a personal or proper designation within that passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Ausē; Afsi.” It does not describe an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept; it identifies an individual. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs two times, both in Numbers 13. The English rendering “Ause” preserves it as a personal name rather than translating it as an ordinary descriptive word.

Achabar is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is also represented as “Akhavar.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:29. Because the available passage text is not included here, the name itself can be explained, but the person’s specific role or significance must be determined from the surrounding biblical context.

Aōd, also rendered Aoth, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it identifies an individual. The name appears 15 times across 14 verses in the Greek Old Testament, with most occurrences in Judges and additional occurrences in Genesis, Exodus, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance belongs to the individuals identified by it in their surrounding passages, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Baithroōb” or “Vethroov.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 10:6. Because no verse text or broader lexical definition is available here, its exact referent must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context rather than from the name alone.

Βεηρα is a proper name, referring to a person identified as Beera or Vira. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available references identify its use in 1 Chronicles 5:6 and 1 Chronicles 7:37, while the precise role of the named person in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Gabatha is a proper name preserved as “Gabatha” or “Gavatha.” In the Greek LXX text, it appears once, in Esther 1:1. Because it is a proper noun rather than a common descriptive word, its main function is to identify a named person, place, or other named entity in the text; the available information does not specify which kind. The exact reference supplies the context needed to determine what it names there.

Galal is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal name. Within the LXX corpus, Galal occurs twice, in 1 Chronicles 9:15 and 1 Chronicles 9:16. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Geddōr” or “Yeththor.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:41. Because the available information does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding passage, the name’s precise referent cannot be explained further here. Its main meaning is its role as a distinctive name preserved in the biblical text.

e.h: Offspring or That Which Is Begotten
e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “that which is begotten; offspring”—those produced or born from another. It refers to descendants or children rather than describing the act of producing them. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Leviticus and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains what has been begotten or brought forth.

This verb means “give relief.” It describes an action that brings relief to someone, presenting relief as something provided rather than merely felt. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Genesis 5:29. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the giving or providing of relief. This is a Greek LXX word, distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary.

This adjective means “red-hot,” describing something heated intensely until it glows or burns with great heat. It is used only twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Daniel and once in 3 Maccabees. The word itself points to an observable condition of extreme heat, while the surrounding sentence determines what object or substance is being described. Its meaning is therefore focused and concrete rather than a broad term for warmth or comfort.

This word means “manage.” It is a verb used for directing or handling something responsibly. Its basic sense is practical: it describes taking charge of a matter and carrying it forward. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice, both times in the book of Wisdom. The surrounding passage determines what is being managed in each occurrence, but the word itself points to the act of managing rather than merely observing or possessing something.

This verb means “on the way through”: traveling or passing through a place during a journey. It describes movement along a route rather than simply being present somewhere. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense applies to repeated descriptions of people or movement passing through lands and regions. The surrounding verse determines who is traveling and what place or route is involved.

This Greek LXX verb means to “bedew” or “besprinkle”—to moisten or sprinkle something with a light covering of liquid. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of lightly moistening or sprinkling.

This word means “trembling” or “shaking.” It is a noun describing the physical condition or movement of trembling rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nahum 2:11. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is trembling there, but the word itself plainly points to quivering or unsteady movement. Its central idea is bodily shaking, whether caused by fear, weakness, or another immediate condition; the word alone does not identify the cause.

This Greek LXX verb means “pluck out”: to pull something out by the roots or from where it is attached. It describes an action of removing something rather than merely touching or moving it. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what is being removed, but its central idea remains forceful extraction.

This Greek LXX verb means “eat up” or “devour,” describing the act of consuming something completely or greedily. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Micah 7:4, so its broader range of use cannot be established from many passages. The surrounding verse supplies the specific force intended there, while the word itself centers on thorough or consuming eating.

Eldad is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is rendered “Eldad,” with “Elthath” also supplied as an associated form. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Numbers: twice in chapter 11 and once in chapter 34. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identification, while the particular role or significance of the person must be understood from each passage.

This word means an earring, an ornament worn on or attached to the ear. It functions as a noun when naming this item, though it can also modify a related noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times across 15 verses, all within the Old Testament corpus. Its uses include earrings associated with personal adornment and with objects given up or removed, but the exact significance depends on the surrounding passage. The word therefore identifies the physical ornament itself rather than expressing a broader spiritual quality or action.

This verb means to deal mercifully with someone—to respond with compassion rather than severity. It describes an act of showing mercy, and its sense is focused on how one person treats another. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 9:8. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise emphasis in that passage must be understood from the wider context. Its basic meaning remains an action of merciful treatment.

This adjective describes something pleasing, gratifying, or agreeable. It can identify what brings satisfaction or what appears welcome and pleasant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse, so its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. The word appears in Job, Proverbs, Obadiah, and Nahum, where readers should understand its basic sense as describing something that gives pleasure or seems agreeable rather than treating it as a technical religious term.

This word means “rust,” referring to the destructive corrosion that forms on metal. It is a noun naming that substance or condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, showing that it is an established term used in several biblical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains rust or corrosion.

This verb means to behave in an orderly fashion. It describes acting with proper arrangement, discipline, or decorum rather than disorder. As a verb, it expresses what someone does, not a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:15. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains conduct that is orderly and well arranged.

This verb means “fit on”—to place or adjust something so that it suits or rests properly upon something else. It describes an action of fitting, rather than merely being suitable in the abstract. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 11:10. Since the verse text is not included here, the specific object being fitted and the exact force of the action must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Zemran is a proper name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Genesis 25:2. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes the person called Zemran from others in the passage. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s role there, but the name itself carries no broader definition in the available record.

This adjective describes something that is tame or has been tamed—made gentle, manageable, or no longer wild. It can describe a person, animal, or thing according to the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is quietness and control rather than untamed behavior. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Esther and once in 2 Maccabees. The exact force in either passage depends on what the adjective describes there.

Thaimanitis, also rendered Themanitis, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). This name occurs once in the LXX, at Job 42:17. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise referent and significance must be determined from that passage’s context.

This Greek LXX verb means “hunt”: to pursue or search for animals as prey. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages connected with hunting animals and obtaining game. Its normal sense remains focused on the deliberate pursuit of prey, while the exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Iekmaam is a proper name, written as “Iekmaam.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 6:53. The name identifies a particular named entity, but the available word-level information does not establish whether that entity is a person, place, or something else. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This verb means “Judaize,” referring to taking on Jewish identity or living in a Jewish manner. As a verb, it describes an action or change rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, in Esther 8:17. Its basic sense identifies the action, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that action is expressed there.

This Greek LXX noun means “purifying.” It refers to something understood by its cleansing or purification function, rather than naming a person or place. In this corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees, at 4 Maccabees 6:29. Its single occurrence gives the word a narrow recorded footprint here, while its central sense remains the act or quality of purifying. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being purified in that passage.

This Greek word means “burn.” It is a verb describing the action of causing something to burn or being consumed by fire, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 76 times, chiefly in passages translated from the Old Testament, and is also found in a small number of deuterocanonical passages. Its use ranges across descriptions involving fire, so the surrounding verse determines what is burning and how the action is taking place. The basic idea remains the same: burning by fire.

This Greek LXX noun means “burnt offering”: a sacrifice presented to God and associated with being burned. It names a sacrificial offering rather than a person, action, or quality. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including Leviticus, Job, and Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the offering.

This adjective describes something that is very dry or parched, lacking moisture. It expresses an intense condition of dryness rather than ordinary dryness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:6. Because the word is an adjective, it describes the condition of a person, object, or land named in the sentence. Its precise emphasis in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: severely dry or parched.

This word means “over against; opposite.” It describes something positioned across from, directly opposite, or in relation to another thing. As an adverb or preposition, it helps express location or direction rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in passages from 2 Samuel, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalms, and Daniel. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and scene.

This Greek LXX verb means “shear” or “crop”: to cut away wool, hair, or similar growth. It describes the act of cutting, especially in connection with shearing animals, rather than merely gathering what has already been cut. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 19 verses, showing repeated use for this practical action. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being cut and the surrounding sentence.

Kenez is a proper name, rendered “Kenez,” used in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 13 times across 13 verses in the LXX corpus, appearing from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise reference in each passage must be understood from the local context. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: Kenez.

This noun means an “omen,” referring to a sign understood as pointing toward or indicating something. It names the perceived sign itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 18:14, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains an omen: a sign treated as meaningful or predictive. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

This noun means “weariness”—a state of becoming tired, exhausted, or burdened by continued effort. It describes depleted strength rather than a particular action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 12:12. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific force there, but the word itself points to the fatigue that can result from labor, effort, or an unending demand.

This verb means “cry out”: to call aloud with a strong, audible voice. It describes a spoken outburst rather than a quiet thought or private feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 3:13. The word itself identifies the action of crying out, while the surrounding passage determines why the person or people cried out and what emotion or purpose accompanied it.

Manthanias is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in the LXX corpus, appearing three times in 1 Chronicles and once in 2 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, these occurrences establish the person’s name but do not by themselves explain his role or significance in each passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to someone called “Marisēs” or “Marisis.” It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Chronicles. The available information identifies the name and its use as a name, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the role connected with the name.

This verb means “scourge”: to subject someone to harsh beating or whipping. It names an action, rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, appearing once in Numbers and twice in later deuterocanonical writings. Its occurrences are found at Numbers 22:25, Wisdom 5:11, and 3 Maccabees 2:21. The surrounding verse determines who performs the action and why, but the word itself refers to the act of scourging.

“Midnight” means the middle point of the night, when one day has ended and the next is beginning. It is a noun naming a specific time, rather than describing a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears four times, each in a different verse, including passages from Judges, Ruth, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it occurs, while the surrounding verse explains what happens at that nighttime hour.

This noun means “rented house,” referring to a dwelling obtained for payment rather than owned outright. It describes a house considered in relation to its rental or occupancy. The word appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, so its basic meaning is connected with a place of residence held by rent. The surrounding passage determines the particular point being made when it appears in a verse.

Mooulathi, also rendered Moulathi, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, object, or quality. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 21:8. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s specific identity and role in that passage cannot be explained further from the word alone.

Naemani is a proper name referring to a person named Naemani. It is preserved as a personal name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), the name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:7. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the role this name has in that passage.

Naphtha is the name of a substance; this word functions as a noun rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:36. The lexical sense is straightforward: it refers to naphtha itself. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the word is being used in that particular passage.

This verb means “spin,” referring to twisting or forming fibers into thread. It describes an action performed with material, rather than a person’s condition or a spoken statement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, all in Exodus, especially in passages describing the making of the tabernacle and its furnishings. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the act of spinning material into usable thread or yarn.

This word means “the.” It is used before a noun or related expression to identify a particular person, thing, or group rather than speaking indefinitely. It can also function alongside a noun-like expression, helping mark what is being referred to in the sentence. This is an extremely common word in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 69,969 times, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its exact English placement may vary with the sentence, but its central role remains identifying a definite referent.

“Likewise” means in the same way or similarly. This adverb connects an action, statement, or situation with something already mentioned, showing that the same kind of thing applies again. It helps readers follow comparison or parallel action without introducing a separate idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 16 times across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what it is linking, but its central function remains clear: it marks correspondence with what came before or with another stated matter.

Oola is a proper name, referring to a specific woman rather than describing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times across four verses, all within Ezekiel 23. The English rendering preserves it as “Oola,” so the word’s primary function is to identify this person. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical meaning itself is simply the woman’s name. The name occurs in Ezekiel 23.4, 23.5, 23.36, and 23.44.

e.h: A Conjunction for Since or That
e.t: This word is a conjunction meaning “since” or “that.” It links one clause to another, introducing either a reason or a statement connected to what comes before. Its role is relational: it helps show how one part of a sentence depends on or explains another, rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books together, it occurs 3,572 times, so its precise force is determined by the surrounding sentence.

Pathoures, also rendered Pathuris, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, in two passages in Jeremiah and two in Ezekiel. Because it functions as a personal or place designation in those passages, its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse text. The name itself does not carry an additional ordinary definition in the available lexical information.

This adjective means “coastal,” describing something connected with the coast or seashore. It identifies a location or feature by its relationship to the shore rather than describing an inland setting. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across six verses, showing a recurring geographical use. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes someone who is a stranger—an outsider or temporary resident rather than a settled member of a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Genesis 23:4 and once in Psalms 38:13. Its central idea is a person living among others without having the status of a native or permanent inhabitant. The surrounding verse determines how that description applies in each passage.

Paschōr, also rendered Paskhor, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs six times in five verses, appearing once in 1 Chronicles and repeatedly in Jeremiah. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the person identified by it; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s role or actions in each occurrence.

This noun means “leg iron”: an iron restraint fastened around a person’s leg. It names a physical device rather than an action, feeling, or personal quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 16 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that the term is used for a real object of restraint. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the iron device itself.

This noun means “surrounding wall,” referring to a wall that encloses or protects an area. It presents the wall as something forming a boundary around what lies within, rather than merely a section of wall. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 2 Kings 25:1 and once in Isaiah 26:1. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains an enclosing wall or fortified boundary.

This Greek LXX verb means to act wickedly or to intend maliciously. It describes purposeful wrongdoing, including a person’s harmful or corrupt intent rather than merely an accidental mistake. The word appears six times in the LXX corpus, in Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, and Susanna. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains deliberate wicked action or malicious purpose.

This word means “old man,” referring to a male person advanced in age. It is a noun, so it identifies the person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 63:9. The basic sense remains focused on age and male identity; the surrounding verse determines why this person is mentioned and what significance the reference has there.

This Greek LXX verb means to “welcome” someone or to “wait for” something with expectation. It describes an active response: receiving a person favorably, or remaining ready for what is anticipated. The word occurs 45 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, so its basic sense is used across a broad range of passages. The surrounding sentence determines whether welcoming or waiting is the clearer emphasis.

This verb means “smell of” or “redolent of.” It describes something as giving off a smell or carrying the characteristic odor of something else. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Psalm 37:6. That reference identifies where the word appears, but the precise force of its use depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic function is to express what something smells of, rather than to name the thing itself.

This verb means “red; inflamed,” describing something that has become reddened or shows inflammation. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used five times, all in Leviticus, in passages dealing with visible changes examined under Israel’s laws concerning skin disease and contaminated materials. The word describes an observable condition rather than naming a disease by itself. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being examined and the surrounding statement. It is rendered “inflamed” in one recorded English translation at Leviticus 13:43.

This word refers to a bramble, a thorny shrub or plant. It is a noun used for a prickly growth rather than for a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, including two occurrences in Judges and one each in Psalms and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its basic sense remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how the plant functions in that passage.

Raphaka, also written Rhafaka, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the travel record of Numbers 33. The available wording identifies the location by name but does not provide an additional definition or description of what the name itself means. Thus, Raphaka refers to a specific place named in Israel’s wilderness journey, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea.

Rōgēl, also identified as “Rhoyil,” is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In English Bible rendering, it appears as Rogel. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 1 Kings. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide surrounding verse text, its specific referent in each passage must be determined from context. It should not be treated as a general word with an everyday definition.

Samaraios, also rendered Samareos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 10:18. Because the available lexical information gives the name but not a broader definition or descriptive sense, its meaning is best understood as identifying the person or group designated by that name in the biblical passage. Its precise referent belongs to the surrounding verse and genealogy.

Seir is a proper name, rendered “Sēir” or “Sir,” rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named person, place, or people in the Old Testament Greek tradition, with its precise referent determined by the surrounding passage. This name occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel, including references in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Joshua.

Sikyōn is a proper name, rendered “Sikyōn” or “Sikion.” As a name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than describing an action or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain which kind of entity it names in that passage.

Siph, also rendered Sif, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament rather than a common descriptive word. It identifies a named person, place, or other specific referent in its passages, though the supplied context does not establish which kind of referent it is. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Judges and 1 Samuel. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Sousan is a proper name rendered as “Susan.” It identifies a person or place by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: once in Nehemiah and three times in Esther. The name itself does not provide a general spiritual or descriptive meaning; its role is to identify the named subject in each passage. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whom or what the name identifies in a particular occurrence.

This word means “drop,” referring to a small amount of liquid. As a noun, it can describe an individual drop or drops considered together. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used nine times, including descriptions rendered as drops and a single drop. Its references span Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Micah, and other books, showing that the word retains this straightforward physical sense across different passages. The surrounding verse determines what liquid or comparison is intended.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut up”: to divide or reduce something by cutting. It describes an action performed on an object or substance, rather than a person’s feeling or attitude. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 12 verses, so its basic sense is established in several parts of the biblical story. The exact object being cut up must be understood from the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains separation or division by cutting.

This noun means a “juncture” or “seam”—the place or line where two parts meet and are joined. It describes connection rather than a separate piece, so the word can refer to the joining point in a constructed object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 26:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the meeting or joining of parts.

This Greek LXX verb means “dine”—to eat a meal. It describes the act of having a meal rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Genesis and once in Proverbs. Its ordinary sense is eating a meal, while its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “system”: an organized arrangement in which parts belong together and function as a whole. It is a noun, so it refers to such an arrangement rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: twice in Old Testament books and twice in Deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being discussed.

Sōchō, also rendered Sokho, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Chronicles 28:18. The name itself identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity in that passage, but the available verse text does not specify which kind. Its precise reference therefore depends on reading the surrounding verse and passage. This word should not be treated as a general term with a broader symbolic meaning.

“Arranged” describes something put in order or set in place. As an adjective, this word characterizes a person, thing, or situation according to how it has been ordered, rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range of use cannot be measured from repeated appearances. Its precise force in Job 12:5 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “triple” or “threefold,” describing something made up of three parts, measures, or layers. It is a Greek LXX word and appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 42:6. The word itself expresses the idea of being three in quantity or arrangement; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described. Its basic meaning is therefore numerical and descriptive rather than an action or personal title.

This noun means “slumber” or “sleep,” referring to the ordinary state of resting or being asleep. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it is used 57 times, describing sleep as a recognizable human condition. Its central meaning remains simple and concrete: a person is sleeping or lies in sleep. The surrounding passage determines whether the word refers to ordinary nighttime rest or sleep in a particular scene.

This Greek LXX verb means to burn by applying fire below something. It describes fire used beneath an object or material, emphasizing the way the burning is done rather than simply stating that something is burning. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Amos, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains burning from underneath.

A weaver is a person who makes cloth by interlacing threads. This Greek LXX noun refers to that craft worker, especially in descriptions of woven materials and their construction. It occurs four times in the LXX, all in Exodus, including passages concerning the tabernacle and priestly clothing. The word identifies the person performing the weaving rather than the cloth or the act itself. Its precise role in any one passage depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means to love knowledge and pursue it. It describes an active desire to seek understanding rather than merely possessing information. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an earnest pursuit of knowledge. The word therefore presents learning as something valued and actively sought.

This Greek LXX verb means to terrify or scare someone—to cause fear or make a person feel threatened. It describes an action directed toward another person, rather than simply naming fear as a feeling. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Ezra and Nehemiah. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its central meaning remains the act of frightening someone.

This word means a “halter,” the strap or bridle used to lead or restrain an animal. It is a noun, so it names the physical object rather than an action. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Job 40:25. Its basic sense is concrete and practical: it refers to equipment placed on an animal for control or guidance. The precise force of the term in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical meaning remains straightforward: a halter.

In its Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 17:17. The word therefore has a specific, concrete sense: raising a mound or setting up a palisade.

This verb means to handle or administer something—to take charge of it, manage it, or direct its use. It describes an active responsibility rather than merely possessing or observing something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains the careful management or direction of what has been entrusted to someone.

This Greek LXX verb means “shine like gold.” It describes giving off a bright, gleaming appearance comparable to gold. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 37:22, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. As a verb, it expresses an action or state of shining rather than naming the object that shines.

This Greek LXX verb means “balk” or “deceive.” It describes misleading someone or frustrating what is true and expected. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 64 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used across many passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.
